== Biography ==

The Queen is the sovereign of Wonderland, ruling from her throne alongside the King. She is celebrated throughout the realm for one distinguishing feature above all others: her ready recourse to the executioner's block. Her judgments are swift and severe. When the Hatter dared to commit the crime of "murdering the time," she "jumped up and bawled out, 'He's murdering the time! Off with his head!'" and has not ceased her clamoring for deaths ever since.

The Queen's executions are not rare occasions but rather the common background of life in Wonderland. During the royal croquet game, which she presides over with absolute authority, she grows "in a furious passion," stamping about the ground and shouting "Off with his head!" or "Off with her head!" with such regularity—"about once in a minute"—that one might mistake it for the rules themselves. Players quarrel and fight, hedgehogs squirm from their places, and soldiers rise and walk off whenever they choose, yet only the Queen's voice remains constant in its demands for beheading.

To meet the Queen is to court danger. When she encounters Alice, she addresses the girl with unmistakable severity, tosses her head impatiently, and dismisses her bluntly as an "Idiot!" for her candid replies. Alice, observing the Queen's manner, understands at once that a single misstep could be fatal. The inhabitants of Wonderland have accepted this as the simple truth of their world: it is "a great wonder" that any of them remain alive at all, given the Queen's enthusiastic fondness for execution.

The Queen's reign is remembered—or dreamed—as a symphony of threats. Her voice, "shrill" and cutting through the chaos of Wonderland, is forever caught in the act of "ordering off her unfortunate guests to execution," a refrain so perfectly suited to her nature that it has become her very character.

== Narrative role ==

The Queen rules Wonderland through fear and the constant threat of execution. A formal invitation bearing her name summons the Duchess to play croquet, and the Duchess abandons all other duties to prepare. The Hatter's account reveals the depth of the Queen's volatile authority: years before, during one of her concerts, she accused him of murdering time itself and ordered his death—a command from which he escaped but at terrible cost, losing his ability to control time forever.

When the Queen's grand procession arrives in the garden, it announces her dominion unmistakably. Alice chooses not to bow, a small defiance that passes without immediate consequence, but the Queen's attention soon turns to her. She interrogates Alice directly and with severity. Nearby, three gardeners had been frantically painting white roses red to hide their mistake, and when the Queen's judgment falls upon them, she sentences them all to execution. Alice, appalled by this injustice, rescues the gardeners by hiding them in a flower-pot—a brave and secret act.

The croquet game that follows becomes a stage for the Queen's temperament. Using live hedgehogs as balls and flamingos as mallets, the game devolves into chaos, and the Queen enters a furious passion. She stamps about, shouting "Off with his head!" or "Off with her head!" so frequently—roughly once each minute—that Alice grows genuinely afraid. From Alice's perspective, the people of Wonderland seem "dreadfully fond of beheading people," leaving her to wonder how any soul survives at all in such a realm. During the game, the Cheshire Cat appears, and Alice confides her deep distress about the Queen's violent nature. When the King befriends the Cat, the Queen immediately orders its execution, setting off a logical debate between the King, Queen, and executioner over whether one can behead a creature without a body. The question remains unresolved as the Cat's head mysteriously disappears.

The Queen's authority and volatility extend beyond the croquet ground. She appears suddenly to threaten the Duchess with execution, forcing the Duchess to flee. She then demands that Alice continue playing croquet, and as the game persists, she orders the execution of the other players one by one, forcing Alice into unwilling participation.

When the trial of the Knave of Hearts convenes—he stands accused of stealing the Queen's tarts—her unpredictable temperament continues to dominate. In the chaos that erupts during the proceedings, the Queen orders the Dormouse removed from the courtroom. The cook, whose examination is to follow, vanishes before the Queen can question her, perhaps anticipating her terrible judgment.

The Queen embodies Wonderland's principle of arbitrary power: swift to condemn, quick to order death, her shrill voice ringing out for blood at every turn—the terrible and absolute rule of a heart that knows only fury and command.

== Personality ==

The Queen's defining characteristic is her violent temperament and absolute intolerance for perceived failure or disrespect. She moves to judgment swiftly and without hesitation, her preferred sentence being execution. Her threats of beheading are so frequent and casual that her subjects regard mere survival in her presence as fortunate. She seems to find savagery not shocking but routine—almost playful in its habitual repetition.

She commands absolute authority through imperious bearing. Those in her presence respond to her with deference and formal obedience; she addresses them directly and without courtesy, dispensing judgments with the certainty of someone unaccustomed to contradiction. When the Knave corrects a mistake, she responds not with measured reproach but with a sharp rebuke, tossing her head impatiently in apparent contempt.

Her anger is performed rather than contained. When displeased, she does not rage in silence but makes her fury loudly known—stamping about, shouting, her voice rising to a shrill pitch that carries and lingers in the memory of those who hear it. This theatrical quality to her wrath, combined with the real consequences of her judgments, makes her presence profoundly unsettling. She seems incapable of small displeasures; every slight calls forth the full force of her indignation.

== Relationships ==

'''[[Alice]]''' — The young visitor and the Queen appear to be natural adversaries, though no open dispute has yet passed between them. Alice, having observed the Queen's terrible swift justice, has grown most uneasy in her presence, knowing that conflict "might happen any minute." This suggests the Queen's volatile nature makes her a danger to all who encounter her.

'''[[King]]''' — The Queen is married to the King of Hearts. They are seated together upon their throne and rule the court jointly, though the Queen seems to hold the greater authority over its proceedings.

'''[[Knave]]''' — The Knave of Hearts seems to stand in some peril from the Queen's mercurial displeasure. When he appeared before her during a procession, she dismissed his bow with disdain, calling him "Idiot!" and tossing her head impatiently in dismissal.

'''[[Hatter]]''' — The Hatter became an object of the Queen's deadly displeasure when he was observed singing at a tea party. Upon hearing him, the Queen leapt up and declared "He's murdering the time!" — calling for his immediate execution.

== Trivia ==

The Queen employs the threat of execution as her primary instrument of governance. She shouts "Off with his head!" or "Off with her head!" with such frequency—about once every minute—that such pronouncements become almost routine to her court.

She interrogates strangers upon first encounter, demanding to know their identity and origins. When encountering Alice, the Queen asks severely "Who is this?" and demands to know "What's your name, child?"

The Queen is swift to anger and prompt to judge. She has addressed even high-ranking courtiers, like the Knave of Hearts, as "Idiot!" when displeased with them, tossing her head impatiently at perceived slights.

Her voice is characteristically shrill and carries with unmistakable authority across Wonderland's strange landscape, recalled as the very voice that orders off her unfortunate guests to execution.

She maintains a peculiar menagerie for her court's entertainments, including a hedgehog employed in her croquet games.
